messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Vikram Patel was fifty-two when an industrial solvent leak transformed a routine warehouse response into a suffocating ordeal. The fire had been banked, but storage tanks had ruptured, flooding the concrete floor with a thick, acrid vapor. As the ventilation system failed, the overhead lights flickered and died, plunging him into a heavy, chemical-laced dark. He remembers the sharp, intoxicating scent of the alcohol-based coolant seeping into his uniform, clinging to his throat. He held his breath, yet the vapor still settled deep in his lungs, and a sudden, animal terror seized him—the visceral certainty that the air itself was becoming poison. He had come to believe that the specific conditions of that afternoon, the failing lights and the rising chemical cloud, were precisely what had trapped him in that moment. When Vikram returned to the paramedic station, the workplace had not lost its familiarity, but it had become a place of quiet tension. The very sight of the ambulance bay, with its narrow corridors and low ceilings, drew the exposure back without warning. A rolling supply cart would scrape across the tile, and suddenly the chemical dark was present again. The smell of the alcohol-based hand sanitizers he applied before every call carried the same sharp weight as the day of the leak, tightening his chest. He learned to move through the station with deliberate steps, as if breathing too deeply might draw the vapor in again. His days settled into a steady rhythm of overlapping habits. He found himself turning the exposure over and over in his mind, tracing the mechanics of the leak and the hours that had passed, certain that a different positioning or an extra layer of protection would have kept the worst at bay. He kept himself constantly surrounded by people so he was never alone with his thoughts, lingering after shifts to speak with dispatch, accepting invitations for coffee, and leaving the television on low at home. At the same time, he began to steer clear of medical cues. Physical examinations felt too clinical, and the sight of ambulances idling at the curb made his pulse quicken. He postponed routine check-ups, telling himself it was simply a matter of timing, though his hands would press lightly against his ribs when the thought of a hospital corridor crossed his mind. Now sixty-one, Vikram remains married and continues to work as a paramedic, though his routine has narrowed to fit his needs. He takes the same district routes, knows the exact doors that will not make the walls feel too close, and carries a small tin of mints to clear the lingering chemical taste from his mouth. The memories do not demand his attention constantly, but when they surface, they arrive with the full force of the original event. He will stop mid-sentence, his shoulders rising, as the terror of that vapor-choked dark returns in a rush. Remembering the event brings back the same terror he felt at the time, overwhelming him with emotion until he has to step away or wait for the feeling to crest. What brought him to seek help this spring was not a sudden crisis, but a quiet realization that he had spent nearly a decade bracing for the dark. He is hoping to reclaim the ease of breathing, to work his shifts without anticipating the recall, and to let the alcohol smell in his workplace simply be a scent rather than a signal.
